profile: Opens each paragraph on the last paragraph's point, often by repeating its key noun: 'Despite saying these words in our munajats…', 'The knowing meant here…', 'Repair is only the start.'
Paragraphs end on the point itself, usually a plain statement, not a flourish: 'That side of the religion is called ʿirfan.', 'In most of us, he says, it is not working.'
Mixed sentence length with short pivot sentences to turn the argument: 'This claim is not contested.', 'Most of us see only the lamp.'

Joins clauses with a bare 'and' but never chains three or more; uses colons for lists and semicolons for contrasts: 'The signs are all around us: in marriage, in the people we meet…'; 'A faculty that exists but has rusted can be repaired; one that is absent cannot…'; 'whereas' once.
Sheikh Bahmanpour named roughly once a paragraph with plain verbs ('says', 'reads it as', 'compares', 'insists', 'explains', 'adds'); 'he says' set as a parenthetical mid-sentence, not as a frame.
A quotation is a short fragment woven into the author's own sentence, then explained in the author's words straight after: '…"There is a machine inside which is [rusted]." That machine is the soul.'
Verses and quotations are led in by one short sentence saying what they do: 'The Qur'an describes the gap in one verse.', 'this is the whole subject in one sentence'.
Reader stance is inclusive 'we/us/most of us' and the occasional 'Let's start with…'/'let's turn to…'; never 'you' in argument, never scolding or presuming.
Plain concrete diction (machine, rusted, red light, lamp); no grand abstractions, no rhetorical questions; questions are reported indirectly ('asks why a believer should bother').
Numbers its steps in plain prose: 'Placing the fault in the receiver has two consequences. The first is… The second is…'; cross-refers to chapters by number ('as Chapter One shows').
Never uses sentence fragments, dramatic suspense, balanced antitheses or quotation stacks (three quoted fragments in one sentence); never ends on an unexplained quotation.

tells: Picks up the preceding image ('as a pupil would'), lead-in sentence before the quotation, 'he says' as mid-sentence parenthetical; slightly tidy close ('gives no other reason for coming') keeps it from higher
Verse lead-ins of one plain sentence ('Surah Fatir describes the same people by what they feel'), 'Most of us' stance, short explanation after the verse
'Then: "These are shirk."' — a dramatic fragment for suspense; Author A never uses fragments, would write 'He then calls them shirk.'
'each in his own words' — filler that adds nothing; Author A would go straight to the teacher and what he says

'tells the traveller that he "has no right…", nor to perform… "does not move on the path…" … "though he may not admit it by word of mouth"' — three quoted fragments stacked, the paragraph ending on an unexplained quotation; Author A quotes one fragment then explains it in his own words
'The prayers go on to ask for three things… Let's take them in turn. The first is sight' — Author A's numbered-steps habit and inclusive 'Let's', with the Sheikh's explanation paraphrased plainly
Opens on the last point ('Familiarity with the words is not the same as…'), 'makes a narrower point' mirrors 'makes the same point'; ends on a quotation without gloss, which lowers it

Colon-led concrete list ('to be in two places at once, to see the future…') and second paragraph picking up 'Pursuing ʿirfan'; summary opening 'This is the case for…' and 'the real thing' are a little looser than the reference
Quotation explained immediately in plain words ('The hadith sets the two kinds of knowing side by side… God places it in the heart') and a one-line lead-in to the next verse

'One addresses the heart of the seeker, the other the eye of the one choosing a guide. Neither makes powers the aim of the path.' — a balanced antithesis plus a summary line to close; Author A ends on the point without a flourish

'"becomes possible at the beginning of spiritual vision", but "the stage of proximity to Allah is far away from this stage" and such things "are not a sign of anybody's being a favorite of Allah"' — three quoted fragments stitched into one sentence; Author A quotes one fragment and glosses it
'Mutahhari's words show why seeking them would be: the goal has become something other than God' — compressed claim-colon-explanation; Author A would write it out as a plain sentence

'shares its root with ʿilm al-huduri' echoes the reference's 'shares its root with maʿrifah'; quotations glossed afterwards ('A result in the laboratory is known because it has been observed'), though that last line is tidier than usual
Cross-reference to 'the rusted faculty that Chapter One described' and the lead-in 'ties the light to the path in one line' match Author A's habits exactly
Mirrors the reference's chapter opening ('These words come from…', 'The line asks God for…') and the 'many of us' stance; argument linked back to Chapter Two in plain prose
'Let's start with…', the Sheikh's question reported indirectly and answered ('In the heart, he answers, it is'), the Arabic term glossed, link back to Chapter One

Numbered gifts ('The second gift… The third gift…') with one-sentence verse lead-ins and the Sheikh's reading paraphrased; the brief comment after the second verse is thinner than Author A usually allows
'Let's start with the two kinds of knowing', Arabic term glossed from its root ('hadd, also means a limit'), 'he adds' parenthetical, concrete example ('the rational animal')

Opens on the last point ('If the faculty can be repaired…'), verse explained with a homely analogy ('a name means little to a person who does not know whom it names'); 'thus' is a touch more formal than the reference
'Reason has a limit and Sheikh Bahmanpour says where it lies' mirrors 'The Qur'an says where it lies'; concrete attributes ('brown or square or useful'), 'In the Sheikh's account'
Each quotation glossed straight after ('In his scheme, what is learned from the jurist begins the circle…', 'His list starts with the heart…'), numbered sequence ('the third')
Semicolon contrast ('There is nothing wrong with…; the trouble is…'), 'as we do', Arabic term glossed after the verse, 'Sheikh Bahmanpour points out' as parenthetical
